lessons.title: Understanding Seed Varieties
lessons.body:
A seed variety is a group of plants with the same characteristics, like fruit size, taste, or days to maturity. When you buy seeds, you will see two main types: hybrid and open-pollinated. Hybrid seeds (often labeled F1) are made by crossing two parent lines. They grow strong and uniform, but you cannot save their seeds for next seasonâthe next generation will be mixed and often poor. Open-pollinated (OP) varieties, including heirloom types, produce seeds that stay true to type if you save them carefully. For example, 'Kilele F1' tomato is a hybrid with high yield and disease resistance, while 'Money Maker' is open-pollinated and can be saved.

Another key difference is days to maturity. A variety like 'Padma' tomato matures in 75 days, while 'Tengeru' takes 90 days. Choose based on your rainy season length. If rains last only 3 months, pick early maturing varieties. Also consider disease resistance. In East Africa, late blight is a big problem for tomatoes. Varieties like 'Meru' and 'Tumaini' have some resistance. For maize, 'DK8031' is drought-tolerant, while 'Pioneer 30G19' is high-yielding but needs more water.

You should also think about market demand. If local buyers want large onions, plant 'Red Creole' or 'Bombay Red'. If they prefer small, pungent ones, grow 'Kitale'. For leafy greens like kale, 'Sukuma Wiki' is common, but 'Thousand Headed' gives more leaves per plant. Always read the seed packet or ask the seller for the variety name, maturity days, and any special notes. Avoid buying seeds without a labelâyou might get a wrong variety that fails.

Finally, test a small plot before planting a whole field. Sow a few seeds of a new variety and see how it performs on your soil and climate. Keep records: planting date, germination rate, pest problems, and yield. After two seasons, you will know which varieties work best for you. Remember, a good variety is the foundation of a healthy nursery and a profitable farm.

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Seeds for Your Region
lessons.body:
Africa has many agro-ecological zones: highlands, dry lowlands, humid forests, and coastal areas. A variety that thrives in one zone may fail in another. Start by knowing your altitude and rainfall. For example, in the highlands above 1,500 meters, you can grow cool-season crops like cabbage, carrots, and potatoes. In lowlands below 1,000 meters, focus on heat-tolerant crops like okra, amaranth, and cowpeas. If you are in a dry area with less than 500 mm of rain per year, choose drought-tolerant varieties like 'Katumani' maize or 'Nerica' rice.

Next, check the length of your growing season. In many parts of Africa, rains come in two seasons. If you have a short rainy season (3-4 months), plant quick-maturing varieties. For beans, 'Rosecoco' takes 90 days, but 'KAT B1' matures in 70 days. For tomatoes, 'Roma VF' takes 75 days, while 'Tanya' takes 90 days. In areas with a long season (6+ months), you can grow long-duration crops like cassava or sweet potatoes.

Soil type also matters. Sandy soils drain fast and need frequent watering. Clay soils hold water but can become waterlogged. If your soil is poor, add compost or manure before planting. Choose varieties that tolerate poor soil, like 'Mwezi Moja' beans or 'Sosuma' sorghum. For acidic soils, which are common in high-rainfall areas, grow acid-tolerant crops like tea, pineapple, or certain potato varieties.

Lastly, talk to local extension officers or experienced farmers. They know which varieties perform well in your area. Visit a nearby research station or agricultural show to see demonstrations. Buy seeds from trusted agro-dealers who stock varieties recommended for your region. The Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) and similar bodies in other countries publish lists of recommended varieties. Using the right seed for your region reduces risk and increases your chances of a good harvest.

lessons.title: Seed Quality Tests: Viability and Germination
lessons.body:
Before you plant, you need to know if your seeds will grow. Two simple tests can save you time and money: the viability test and the germination test. Viability tells you if the seed is alive; germination tells you what percentage will sprout. You can do both at home with minimal tools.

For a quick viability test, drop seeds in a glass of water. Good seeds sink; dead or hollow seeds float. This works well for beans, maize, and sunflower. But for small seeds like tomato or onion, use the rag-doll test. Moisten a piece of cloth or paper towel, place 10 seeds evenly, roll it up, and keep it warm and damp. Check after 5-7 days. Count how many have sprouted. If 8 out of 10 sprout, your germination rate is 80%. For a more accurate test, use a seed tray with sterile soil. Plant 100 seeds, keep moist, and count seedlings after 10-14 days. A germination rate above 80% is good; below 60% means you should buy new seeds.

Another test is the float test for specific crops. For maize, put seeds in water with a pinch of salt. Good seeds sink; bad ones float. For rice, use a salt solution (1 part salt to 10 parts water). Viable seeds sink. Always rinse seeds after float tests to remove salt.

You can also check seed vigor by pressing a seed with your fingernail. If it is hard and plump, it is likely viable. If it crumbles or is soft, it is dead. For large seeds like beans, cut one open. A healthy seed has a white, creamy embryo. A black or brown embryo means it is dead.

Record your results. If germination is low, increase seeding rate. For example, if you need 100 plants and germination is 70%, sow 143 seeds (100 divided by 0.7). Always test seeds from new sources or from your own saved seeds. This simple step prevents empty nurseries and wasted labor.

lessons.title: Seed Sources and Certification
lessons.body:
Where you buy your seeds matters as much as the variety. In Africa, you can get seeds from several sources: agro-dealers, research stations, NGOs, fellow farmers, and your own saved seeds. Each has pros and cons. Certified seeds from agro-dealers are tested for quality and are usually free of pests and diseases. They come in sealed packets with labels showing variety, germination rate, and lot number. Always check the expiry date. For example, a packet of 'H614D' maize from Kenya Seed Company should have a germination rate of at least 85% and be less than one year old.

Research stations like KALRO in Kenya, TARI in Tanzania, and NARO in Uganda produce foundation and certified seeds. They also sell small packs to farmers. NGOs sometimes distribute free or subsidized seeds, especially after disasters. But be careful: free seeds may not be the best variety for your area, and they may be older. Always ask for the variety name and planting instructions.

Farmer-saved seeds are cheap and adapted to local conditions, but they can carry diseases and have low germination. If you save seeds, select from your healthiest plants, harvest at full maturity, and dry properly. For cross-pollinated crops like maize, you must isolate to avoid mixing varieties. For self-pollinated crops like beans and tomatoes, saving is easier.

Certification is a system where a government agency inspects seed production and tests quality. Certified seed bags have a blue or green label with details. In Kenya, the Kenya Plant Health Inspectorate Service (KEPHIS) certifies seeds. In Tanzania, it is the Tanzania Official Seed Certification Institute (TOSCI). Look for the label. Avoid buying seeds from open buckets or unlabeled containersâthey could be fake or expired. If you buy from a new seller, ask for a receipt and test a small sample before planting your whole field. Good seeds are an investment, not an expense.

lessons.title: Seed Storage Best Practices
lessons.body:
Proper storage keeps seeds alive from one season to the next. The three enemies of seeds are moisture, heat, and pests. If you store seeds in a damp, hot place, they will die or rot. Aim for a cool, dry, dark place. A temperature of 10-15Â°C and relative humidity below 50% is ideal. In many African homes, this means storing seeds in sealed containers in the coolest room, away from the kitchen fire.

Start by drying seeds well. Sun-dry seeds on a mat for 2-3 days until they are crisp. For maize, the kernel should crack when bitten, not dent. For beans, the seed should shatter when hit with a hammer. After drying, put seeds in an airtight container. Glass jars with rubber seals, plastic buckets with tight lids, or metal cans work well. Add a desiccant like silica gel or dry wood ash to absorb moisture. You can also use dry rice grains: put a handful in a cloth bag and place it in the container.

To prevent pests, mix seeds with natural repellents. For every 10 kg of seed, add 100 g of dry neem leaves or 50 g of wood ash. For maize, you can use actellic dust (follow label instructions). Store different crops separately to avoid mixing and cross-contamination. Label each container with crop name, variety, and date of storage.

Check your seeds every 2-3 months. Look for mould, insects, or a musty smell. If you see weevils, sun-dry the seeds again and clean the container. For small quantities, you can store seeds in the refrigeratorâbut let them warm to room temperature before planting to avoid condensation.

Never store seeds in plastic bags that are not sealed, as moisture can enter. Also, keep seeds away from chemicals like fertiliser or petrol. With good storage, seeds can remain viable for 2-3 years for most crops, and up to 5 years for beans and maize. Always test germination before planting stored seeds.

lessons.title: Handling Hybrid and Open-Pollinated Seeds
lessons.body:
Hybrid and open-pollinated (OP) seeds require different handling. Hybrid seeds are the result of controlled crosses between two distinct parent lines. They are expensive but give higher yields, uniform growth, and better disease resistance. However, you cannot save seeds from hybrid plants for replanting. The next generation will be a mix of traits, often with lower yield and poor quality. For example, if you plant hybrid tomato 'Kilele F1' and save its seeds, the resulting plants may produce small, tasteless fruits. So for hybrids, you must buy new seeds each season.

Open-pollinated seeds, on the other hand, can be saved and replanted. They are cheaper and often more adaptable to local conditions. But to keep the variety pure, you must prevent cross-pollination with other varieties of the same crop. For example, if you grow two varieties of maize close together, they will cross-pollinate and the saved seeds will be mixed. To avoid this, plant different varieties at least 200 meters apart, or plant them at different times so they flower at different times. For crops like beans and tomatoes, which self-pollinate, isolation distance can be smaller (10-20 meters).

When saving OP seeds, select from your best plants. Choose plants that are healthy, productive, and have the traits you want. Harvest seeds from mature fruits or pods. For tomatoes, scoop out seeds, ferment them in water for 2 days to remove the gel, then rinse and dry. For beans, let pods dry on the plant, then shell and store. For maize, leave cobs on the plant until fully dry, then shell.

Always label your saved seeds with the variety name and date. Store them properly. If you are new to seed saving, start with easy crops like beans, tomatoes, and peppers. Avoid saving seeds from crops that cross-pollinate easily, like maize, unless you can isolate them. Remember, hybrid seeds are a recurring cost, while OP seeds can be a long-term resource if managed well. Choose based on your budget, market, and farming goals.

quiz.q: What does 'F1' on a seed packet indicate?
quiz.explanation: F1 stands for first filial generation, which is a hybrid produced by crossing two parent lines.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of open-pollinated seeds?
options: A) They cannot be saved for replanting
B) They always give higher yields than hybrids
C) Their seeds can be saved and replanted
D) They are always more expensive than hybrids
quiz.explanation: Open-pollinated seeds produce offspring that are similar to the parent, so they can be saved and replanted.

quiz.q: If you need 100 plants and your seed germination rate is 70%, how many seeds should you sow?
quiz.explanation: Divide the desired number of plants by the germination rate: 100 / 0.7 = 143 seeds.

quiz.q: Which factor is most important when choosing a seed variety for your region?
options: A) The color of the seed packet
B) The price of the seeds
C) The altitude and rainfall of your area
D) The brand name of the seed company
quiz.explanation: Altitude and rainfall determine which crops and varieties will grow well in your specific agro-ecological zone.

quiz.q: What is the float test used for?
options: C) To test seed germination rate
quiz.explanation: The float test quickly checks if seeds are alive; viable seeds usually sink, while dead or hollow seeds float.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good storage practice for seeds?
options: A) Store in a damp place
B) Store in an airtight container with a desiccant
D) Store in a plastic bag with no seal
quiz.explanation: Airtight containers with a desiccant keep seeds dry and viable by preventing moisture damage.

quiz.q: What does a seed certification label guarantee?
options: A) The seeds are the cheapest available
B) The seeds have been tested for quality and are free from pests
C) The seeds are genetically modified
D) The seeds will grow in any region
quiz.explanation: Certification ensures seeds meet quality standards, including germination rate and freedom from pests and diseases.

quiz.q: Why should you not save seeds from hybrid plants?
options: A) They are illegal to save
B) The next generation will be uniform and high-yielding
C) The next generation will be mixed and often poor
D) They will not germinate at all
quiz.explanation: Hybrid seeds are genetically unstable; saved seeds from hybrids produce offspring with unpredictable and often inferior traits.

quiz.q: What is the ideal relative humidity for seed storage?
quiz.explanation: Low humidity (below 50%) prevents mould and keeps seeds dry and viable.

quiz.q: Which crop is easiest for a beginner to save seeds from?
quiz.explanation: Beans are self-pollinating and their seeds are easy to harvest and store, making them ideal for beginners.

quiz.q: What is a sign that maize seeds are properly dried for storage?
options: A) They are soft when pressed
C) They are green in color
quiz.explanation: Properly dried maize kernels are hard and crack when bitten, indicating low moisture content.

quiz.q: How often should you check stored seeds?
quiz.explanation: Checking every 2-3 months allows you to detect mould, insects, or moisture problems early.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of fermenting tomato seeds before storage?
options: A) To make them taste better
B) To remove the gel that inhibits germination
quiz.explanation: Fermentation removes the gel sac around tomato seeds, which contains germination inhibitors and can cause disease.

quiz.q: Which of these is a hybrid variety?
quiz.explanation: Kilele F1 is a hybrid tomato, as indicated by the 'F1' label.

quiz.q: What is the minimum isolation distance for saving seeds from cross-pollinated crops like maize?
quiz.explanation: To prevent cross-pollination, maize varieties should be separated by at least 200 meters or planted at different times.

quiz.q: Which organization certifies seeds in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: KEPHIS (Kenya Plant Health Inspectorate Service) is responsible for seed certification in Kenya.

quiz.q: What is a good natural repellent for storing seeds against pests?
quiz.explanation: Dry neem leaves are a natural insect repellent that can be mixed with stored seeds.

quiz.q: What does a germination rate of 60% mean?
options: A) 60 out of 100 seeds will sprout
B) 60% of the seeds are dead
C) The seeds are 60 days old
D) The seeds will take 60 days to mature
quiz.explanation: Germination rate is the percentage of seeds that sprout under ideal conditions; 60% means 60 out of 100 seeds sprout.

quiz.q: Which of these is a drought-tolerant maize variety?
quiz.explanation: DK8031 is known for its drought tolerance, making it suitable for dry areas.

quiz.q: Why should you label stored seeds?
options: A) To make them look pretty
B) To know the variety and storage date
quiz.explanation: Labeling helps you identify the variety and know how long the seeds have been stored, which affects viability.

quiz.q: What is the rag-doll test used for?
quiz.explanation: The rag-doll test is a simple method to check germination by placing seeds in a moist cloth and counting sprouts.

quiz.q: Which of these is a self-pollinating crop?
quiz.explanation: Tomatoes are self-pollinating, meaning they do not require cross-pollination to produce seeds.

quiz.q: What should you do before planting seeds stored in a refrigerator?
options: B) Let them warm to room temperature
C) Soak them in hot water
quiz.explanation: Letting refrigerated seeds warm to room temperature prevents condensation and shock, improving germination.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of certified seeds?
options: B) They are guaranteed to be high quality and disease-free
C) They can be saved for many seasons
quiz.explanation: Certified seeds undergo quality checks, ensuring high germination and freedom from pests and diseases.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of dead seeds?
options: B) They are hard and plump
D) They have a white embryo when cut open
quiz.explanation: Dead or hollow seeds often float in water, while viable seeds usually sink.

quiz.q: What is the recommended storage temperature for seeds?
quiz.explanation: A cool temperature of 10-15Â°C helps maintain seed viability by slowing down metabolic processes.

quiz.q: Why is it important to test germination before planting?
options: A) To know how many seeds to sow
B) To determine the seed variety
C) To check the seed color
quiz.explanation: Germination rate tells you what percentage of seeds will sprout, so you can adjust seeding rate to get the desired plant population.

quiz.q: Which of these is an open-pollinated variety?
quiz.explanation: Money Maker is an open-pollinated tomato variety, so its seeds can be saved and replanted.

quiz.q: What is a desiccant used for in seed storage?
quiz.explanation: A desiccant like silica gel absorbs moisture from the air, keeping seeds dry during storage.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find weevils in stored seeds?
options: B) Sun-dry the seeds and clean the container
D) Store them in a plastic bag
quiz.explanation: Sun-drying kills weevils and their eggs, and cleaning the container prevents reinfestation.
